user_input: What is the business model of Cheesecake Factory Inc?
reference: Cheesecake Factory Inc operates a mix of company-operated and licensed locations. For company-operated restaurants, they pay upfront costs and receive an average 20-25% cash-on-cash return from those locations. For licensed locations, the company does not require any capital expenditure but receives development fees and ongoing royalty fees.
reference_contexts: Company Overview As the company describes in their latest 10-K filing: The Cheesecake Factory restaurants strive to provide a distinctive, high-quality dining experience at moderate prices by offering an extensive, innovative and evolving menu in an upscale casual, high-energy setting with attentive, efficient and friendly service. As a result, The Cheesecake Factory restaurants appeal to a diverse customer base across a broad demographic range. Our extensive menu and strategic selection of locations enable us to compete for substantially all dining preferences and occasions, from the key lunch and dinner day parts to the mid-afternoon and late-night day parts, which are traditionally weaker times for most casual dining restaurants, as well as special occasion dining. The Cheesecake Factory restaurants are generally open seven days a week for lunch and dinner, and we offer additional menu items for weekend brunch. Most of Cheesecake Factory Inc’s restaurants, including their namesake The Cheesecake Factory chain, target the upscale casual market, meaning fancier than casual but not as fancy as fine dining. For example, here’s what their The Cheesecake Factory interiors look like: Source: Cheesecake Factory October 2019 Presentation The Cheesecake Factory locations tend to be large and very busy, especially during the late night when many other restaurants are winding down. They have extremely broad menus, more than most restaurants, including steak, chicken, burgers, seafood, pizza, pasta, sandwiches, salads, and so forth. I personally don’t like that; I prefer restaurants that have a narrow menu that they specialize in, and for example I think The Cheesecake Factory’s steaks are rather poor compared to a proper steakhouse. However, a broad menu seems to have been working well for The Cheesecake Factory, because a whole family or dining group can find something they like on the menu. Naturally, The Cheesecake Factory specializes in dessert, and gets 16% of sales from dessert, which is much higher than most restaurants. While much of their menu is not particularly special in my view, their desserts are broadly considered to be exceptional. I don’t even particularly like cheesecake but I still like theirs. Over the past several years, third-party app-based delivery providers have expanded the restaurant’s reach. In 2009 they received 9% of sales from delivery orders, but in 2018 it was up to 14%. This is also a competitive threat, though, because delivery food via third-party apps has lower margins than dine-in eating. The company has 202 The Cheesecake Factory locations in the United States and one in Canada that are company-operated. The management team believes that they can eventually expand to 300 locations in the United States and 10 in Canada. The closest location to my home is approximately 1 hour away, for example. The only location I have visited is in Florida whenever I visit family there (they love the restaurant and brought my attention to it). I have close friends that have visited multiple locations throughout the northeast USA. The company also has 24 locations that operate in Mexico, the Middle East, and China that are licensed to third-party operators, with the first one having opened in 2012. There are currently three licensee operators of those 24 locations. The biggest licensee by far is based in Kuwait and has 16 locations throughout multiple Middle East countries and rights/options to expand into eastern Europe. They also can expand into Egypt, which is a huge 100 million population market with a lot of potential. I was in Egypt during much of October visiting family, and malls and restaurants there (often developed operators from Gulf states like Kuwait) are absolutely booming, and many of them have American restaurant brands like Chili’s. I could easily see a bunch of The Cheesecake Factory locations sprinkled into the mix; they would fit right into the higher-end development complexes. Another licensee is based in Mexico, currently has four locations in Mexico, and has rights/options to expand elsewhere in Latin America. The third licensee is based in Hong Kong, with four locations in China, and has rights/options for multi-country Asian expansion. With company-operated restaurants, the company pays the upfront costs and receives an average 20-25% cash-on-cash return from those locations. For licensed locations, the company doesn’t require any capital expenditure. Instead, they receive development fees and ongoing royalty fees, and they have a team dedicated to helping the licensed operators create and operate the locations in line with the company’s standards. The company reports that each international licensed location adds about $0.01 to the stock’s overall EPS. The company has internally developed and deployed a small number of other restaurant chains, including Grand Lux Cafe, Social Monk Asian Kitchen, and RockSugar Southeast Asian Kitchen. Lastly, they now also have over 21 North Italia restaurant locations, and 48 diverse restaurants within their recently-acquired FRC brand that I’ll get into later in this report.

There’s often a curve ball or black swan somewhere, and this time it was a virus. Many pundits on CNBC and other media outlets seem to think that the economy was doing just fine before this hit, but that was not the case. Corporate profit growth was 0% in 2019, and excluding buybacks and tax cuts has been flat for several years before the involvement of trade wars or viruses. Debt levels are near record highs, and the bottom half of the U.S. population is deeply financially insecure, more than they have been historically. The U.S. government deficit as a percentage of GDP has been rising dramatically since 2016; it’s supposed to shrink during a strong economy. The Systemic Debt Issue The United States reached a peak total debt (public + private) at 380% of GDP in 2009. That was our all-time record high. More specifically, the U.S. entered that recession with a total debt/GDP ratio of a bit under 350%, and it grew to 380% during the process. After a period of modest deleveraging, mainly in the housing sector, we’re currently back down to just under 350% debt to GDP. So, we’re entering this likely recession with a similar level of debt as 2007. The Great Depression of 1929 and the Great Recession of 2008 were so severe in part because debt levels were so historically high. Those two periods are “special” in terms of how rapidly the monetary base was expanded to deal with them compared to every other recession. This is a chart of the U.S. monetary base in log form, so every move up is exponential and this makes it easier to see the differences between normal exponential growth and accelerated exponential growth. The company just completed the merger-acquisition of its parent company at the start of this month, which creates one of the largest banks in the world by market capitalization. Company and Merger Background The Housing Development Finance Corporation (generally known as HDFC) was founded in 1977 and has been a primary financier of real estate in India. From the country’s independence in 1947 until the early 1990s, India had a partially socialist economics model (state-directed and protectionist), and had rather slow structural growth. In the early 1990s, there were a series of reforms to liberalize and open up the economy to the world more broadly, and to incorporate more market-oriented aspects. Growth has been stronger ever since. As part of this shift, HDFC launched HDFC Bank as a subsidiary in 1994. HDFC continued focusing on real estate finance, insurance, asset management, and a few other areas, while HDFC Bank remained partly owned by HDFC and grew into the largest bank in the country. HDFC retained some of the shares as a partial parent company. In 2022, it was announced that HDFC Bank would acquire-merge its parent HDFC into itself, to create a more streamlined full-service banking giant. Early this month, that merger completed ahead of schedule. In addition to streamlining the overhead costs and corporate structure, one of the biggest opportunities that comes from the merger is the ability to cross-sell HDFC’s products to HDFC Bank customers. HDFC Bank has around 83 million customers but only 2% have a housing loan with HDFC. An additional 5% of the bank’s customers have a housing loan from other lenders, he said explaining that it means 93% of HDFC Bank’s customers do not have a home loan. This presents a “significant opportunity to cross sell and a potential to tap into the customer base that have not taken a housing loan at all,” the director said, adding that HDFC Bank will now be able to offer mortgage services. Mortgage penetration in India is “extremely low” and only accounts for approximately 11% of its GDP. That’s much lower than 26% in China, and between 20% to 40% in South East Asia, HDFC said. Most developed markets have more than 50% mortgage penetration, the company added. –CNBC, July 4th 2023 India is one of the fastest-growing countries in the world in terms of real GDP, and the financial sector of the country is growing even faster than overall GDP, because India is starting from a baseline that is under-banked compared to its peers. In other words, each country’s central bank runs its own local ledger, but then to varying degrees most of them tie into the U.S. Federal Reserve’s ledger by a combination of 1) dollar-denominated international pricing contracts, 2) holding dollar-denominated reserve assets, and 3) using dollar-denominated financing (debts). This gives the U.S. the ability to freeze their funds, sanction them from using the ledger, etc. And it’s mainly based on the post-WWII environment where the U.S. was the sole hyperpower. Now that China has grown considerably, and the world economy is more distributed overall, there are natural calls for a more balanced or distributed global payment system as well. For example, should Saudi Arabia continue to only sell oil in dollars, even though China is by far its biggest customer now, rather than the United States? But talk is easier than action; monies and financial systems have significant network effects and high switching costs. China and its partners have serious scale to create an alternative system, but it’s a massive undertaking. China and India aren’t even on great geopolitical terms, for starters. There were some analysts, generally from the gold enthusiast community, expecting the announcement of a shared currency backed by gold, which didn’t materialize. Instead, what we should expect out of BRICS is a gradual piecemeal coalition to align their payment systems. To the extent that they de-dollarize, it will be due to various currency swaps, commodity contracts, and so forth to use the major currencies of the bloc, especially the Chinese yuan. And with that, we will probably see continued gradual diversification of reserve holdings. In addition to network effects around payment rails and currency liquidity, impediments to the yuan meaningfully displacing the dollar are 1) capital controls and 2) a lack of attractive securities to hold relative to what’s available in U.S. capital markets. The latter has been a consistent problem for the Eurozone as well, since multiple different smaller semi-liquid capital markets are less attractive than one giant liquid capital market. I expect some meaningful degree of de-dollarization and global currency diversification in the decade ahead, but it will become overhyped for periods of time, and analysts will likely keep mistaking words for actions. Actions are what matter. The news that did come out of the BRICS summit is that six new members will join on January 1, 2024. These nations include Argentina, Egypt, Ethiopia, Saudi Arabia, Iran, and the UAE. They are in light blue on Wikipedia’s useful map below: -Saudi Arabia, Iran, and the UAE are very important entrants, because they are major oil producers. In addition, Saudi Arabia and Iran have a history of geopolitical animosity, which has been a main catalyst for the close relationship between the U.S. and Saudi Arabia. Over the past couple of years, China has served as the peacemaker between the two countries, and their formal inclusion into BRICS helps further cement that pragmatic peace. -Egypt is another major inclusion, with a population of nearly 110 million people, control over the extremely strategically important Suez Canal, and a military ranking that is considered around #14 globally. I’m currently in Egypt, and people I know here who do not normally focus on financial matters have been highly interested in Egypt’s BRICS inclusion. They see it as a way to escape from the yoke of U.S. financial and geopolitical imperialism, and to align with a broader coalition. (I do, however, expect another round of devaluation for the Egyptian currency over the next year or so.) -Argentina’s inclusion is at least somewhat in question at this time, because while their establishment leaders want to be included and the formal plan is to join, their rising populist leaders generally do not favor BRICS. In particular, Javier Milei came out ahead in Argentina’s August 2023 primary election, and he has a less favorable view of BRICS than his political peers. Should he win the autumn presidential 2023 election, it’s unclear if this would affect Argentina’s BRICS inclusion. Overall, the BRICS alignment represents a major alternative to the US/Europe/Australia/Japan alignment, and whether in this name or another name (e.g. the Shanghai Cooperation Organization) will likely represent a defining geopolitical bipolar power competition in the years ahead. However, major global financial changes take time, due to serious network effects and complexities.

Normally the group of oil-producing nations that collectively make up OPEC, along with their partnership with Russia, would cut oil production to preserve higher oil prices, to balance supply with demand. It is the perfect storm for the energy market, and a truly historic moment, because oil demand is weak and oil supply will now be maximized. This is a scorched-earth attempt to take market share back by bankrupting many higher-cost or indebted producers worldwide, and is particularly damaging to the weaker half of U.S. shale oil producers. It’s the opposite this time; U.S. banks are quite well capitalized with plenty of reserves due to all the changes since 2008. Tons of businesses are already drawing on their revolving credit facilities from banks, meaning they are pulling extra cash from banks onto their balance sheets to deal with whatever comes next. Some obvious companies like Boeing and Hyatt are raising cash, but even companies with strong balance sheets and plenty of cash already like Micron (a big RAM/NAND semiconductor producer) are tapping into their facilities to maximize cash levels even further. This puts a lot of pressure on the banking system. Just like how banks are not designed to hand out cash deposits to all of their customers at once, they are not designed to fulfill all of their client revolving credit facilities at once. The FRA/OIS spread, which is a measure of interbank liquidity, spiked this past week to levels not seen since 2008, meaning there is a serious liquidity problem. The Fed initially tried to address this liquidity problem, along with the liquidity problem that was happening in the Treasury market (which really is all part of the same issue) by announcing literally trillions of dollars in open repo lending lines going forward, which is the biggest ever such move, but that didn’t work at all. Banks only borrowed a small portion of that, roughly $100 billion, despite their rising liquidity problems. This seems to have to do with regulations; repo liquidity (which is borrowed rather than permanent) is not going to cut it. The dollar index started to spike and was briefly relieved when the Fed announced that liquidity bazooka, but it was temporary relief for about a day as market participants realized that it didn’t work and that it never entered the system. Macro View The Strait of Hormuz As we wrap up the 8th week of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, it remains the largest variable in the global macroeconomic situation. Since my prior report, military activity has gone down substantially amid ceasefire discussions, but with little tangible progress between US and Iran. Demand destruction is taking hold, where many poorer countries experience energy curfews, mild-to-moderate energy rationing, and so forth. Fertilizer and food prices are up. Consumers and businesses in the US and other wealthy nations are generally avoiding shortages, but are paying higher prices, which eats into potential spending elsewhere in the economy and contributes to record-low consumer sentiment. The longer the issue drags on, the more impactful it is likely to become. Since the start of April, the US began drawing down some of its strategic petroleum reserve to offset the issue. It’s a small total number so far, but large on a weekly change basis: China, the US, and Japan all have rather sizable reserves. On the other hand, Europe’s is pretty small relative to their economic and population size, even though they still do import most of theirs like Japan does. Another big issue is jet fuel. A barrel of oil is ultimately refined into a number of different types of fuel, and one of them is kerosene, used for air travel. That particular type of fuel is running into more shortages than other types at this early stage, resulting in many airlines cancelling unprofitable flight routes. We often hear the number that about 20% of the world’s oil and other liquid fuels passes through the Strait of Hormuz. However, that’s an aggregate number, and there are many nuances within it. The head of the International Energy Agency, for example, has pointed out that Europe gets 75% of its jet fuel from the Middle East: Middle East refineries provide Europe with around 75% of Europe’s jet fuel but production from those facilities “is basically now almost zero,” he added. –CNBC, April 23rd 2026 Additionally, jet fuel demand rises in the summer months, meaning that the supply-demand mismatch has the potential to sharply worsen if the supply-side Hormuz situation remains unresolved by then. swap lines with the US (Bank of England, European Central Bank, Bank of Japan, Swiss National Bank, and Bank of Canada), but others are occasionally given swap lines during severely adverse conditions (such as Covid, where up to 14 countries had swap lines temporarily). The reasons I don’t consider these recent swap lines headlines to be as serious as many took them to be are twofold. First, the UAE and most other nations that reportedly asked for swap lines have high levels of foreign-exchange reserves. They could trim those reserves to backstop their currencies. Second, the Fed already has a standing “Foreign and International Monetary Authorities (FIMA) repo facility”, which lets foreign central banks pledge their treasuries as collateral for dollars, rather than sell them. They put this in place during Covid and it reduces the need for swap lines in general: The Federal Reserve established a repurchase agreement facility for foreign and international monetary authorities (FIMA Repo Facility). By creating a backstop source of temporary dollar liquidity for FIMA account holders, the facility can help address pressures in global dollar funding markets that could otherwise affect financial market conditions in the United States. Its role as a liquidity backstop also helps to support the smooth functioning of financial markets more generally. The FIMA Repo Facility allows FIMA account holders, which consist of central banks and other international monetary authorities with accounts at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, to enter into repurchase agreements with the Federal Reserve. In these transactions, approved FIMA account holders temporarily exchange their U.S. Treasury securities held with the Federal Reserve for U.S. dollars, which can then be made available to institutions in their jurisdictions. This facility provides, at a backstop rate, an alternative temporary source of U.S. dollars for foreign official holders of Treasury securities other than sales of the securities in the open market. A temporary FIMA Repo Facility was established March 31, 2020, and the facility was made a standing facility on July 28, 2021. –Federal Reserve These types of swap lines and repo facilities are not provided to the world out of benevolence. Rather, they are provided to the world so that international entities don’t have to rapidly sell treasuries and cause market disruption to our bond market whenever they have temporary extra liquidity needs. They’re standing facilities that exist primarily for this purpose. As I’ve said before, certain smaller developing countries could certainly be facing acute or semi-acute dollar shortages at the moment, and likely are. However, those are local problems rather than ones that rise up to a global macro level, as would be the case when larger, wealthier nations run into shortages.

Importantly, unlike Europe and Japan, Canada and the Latin American markets that Scotiabank operates in have positive yield curves. Whenever it goes up, it means value stocks are globally outperforming growth stocks, and whenever it goes down, it means growth stocks are outperforming: Looking back historically longer-term, periods of higher inflation correspond to value stocks generally outperforming growth stocks. This was true in the 1940s, the 1970s, and the 2000s. On the value side, commodity producers benefit from higher prices and banks benefit from positive yield curves. On the growth side, the growth/tech companies do fine fundamentally, but their valuations get pressured from higher inflation and higher long-end interest rates. As an example of the type of growth stocks that are on the other side of that growth-to-value rotation, we can see examples like Cadence Design Systems (CDNS) that rolled over but are still very pricey by historical standards: Chart Source: F.A.S.T. Graphs Basically, companies like Cadence are great in terms of underlying fundamentals, but became quite overheated in terms of valuation in 2020. Cadence trades at a forward estimated price/earnings/growth ratio (“PEG ratio”) of 4x. And despite being a mature company, it still doesn’t pay a dividend. While there are select growth stocks I own and would buy on corrections, I continue to prefer a value tilt at this time. There are plenty of good companies in the healthcare sector, financial sector, and energy sector that remain at below-average valuations despite in many cases having improved their underlying quality in a difficult disinflationary environment over the past several years. As governments taper stimulus, banks could face more headwinds. However, I think that there is a feedback function here; any slowness of growth and return of disinflation and solvency problems, has a good chance of stirring up another round of fiscal support. At this stage of the long-term debt cycle with rising populism, policymakers have a tight response time towards economic issues. Scotiabank has exposure to Canada’s expensive housing market, but less-so than some of their rival banks which is why it is my preferred Canadian bank. Instead, Scotiabank has diversified into Latin America via Mexico, Chile, Peru, and Columbia. That’s a combination that I like quite a bit because it gives investors curated emerging market exposure through a developed market bank. Unlike credit risk which hits hard and fast, interest rate risk slowly bleeds the banks of profitability over time. Banks don’t do well in zero-rate or negative-rate environments, and tend to prefer steeper yield curves. European and Japanese banks have been absolutely crushed by low rate policy for decades now. The Banking Sector Back in 2008, banks themselves were undercapitalized, so they crashed harder than the broader economy. It’s the opposite this time; U.S. banks are quite well capitalized with plenty of reserves due to all the changes since 2008. However, the broader corporate sector is highly indebted and many industries will be hit by economic shutdowns (airlines, hotels, oil producers, restaurant chains, movie theaters, malls, concert venues, anything tourism related, etc). Tons of businesses are already drawing on their revolving credit facilities from banks, meaning they are pulling extra cash from banks onto their balance sheets to deal with whatever comes next. Some obvious companies like Boeing and Hyatt are raising cash, but even companies with strong balance sheets and plenty of cash already like Micron (a big RAM/NAND semiconductor producer) are tapping into their facilities to maximize cash levels even further. This puts a lot of pressure on the banking system. Just like how banks are not designed to hand out cash deposits to all of their customers at once, they are not designed to fulfill all of their client revolving credit facilities at once. The FRA/OIS spread, which is a measure of interbank liquidity, spiked this past week to levels not seen since 2008, meaning there is a serious liquidity problem. The Fed initially tried to address this liquidity problem, along with the liquidity problem that was happening in the Treasury market (which really is all part of the same issue) by announcing literally trillions of dollars in open repo lending lines going forward, which is the biggest ever such move, but that didn’t work at all. One of the biggest components of my analysis over the past 6-7 years has been about the growing impact of fiscal dominance in the United States. Nothing stops this (fiscal) train. The tangible takeaway from it is that I would consistently predict 1) large fiscal deficits despite verbal attempts by policymakers to reduce them and 2) that those large fiscal deficits would be greatly beneficial to asset prices despite other bearish concerns along the way.
